title: Tier routing T1 core
desc: T1 core decision rules + WillKim standing orders for agent dispatch. Next: claude-code-agent-tier-routing-howto (briefing/dispatch recipes); claude-code-agent-tier-routing-ref (preamble/glossary/lessons).
steps: NAVIGATION: T1 core decision rules + WillKim standing orders. Briefing recipes, dispatcher syntax, conductor patterns, fan-out execution rules: wkappbot skill read claude-code-agent-tier-routing-howto. Constitutional preamble, glossary, history, samjil-prevention lessons, dated incident history: wkappbot skill read claude-code-agent-tier-routing-ref.

TIER SELECTION: chores (grep/read/survey/pattern search) -> Haiku Agent tool. Source splits/multi-file refactors/code restructuring -> Codex ONLY (never Haiku -- it silently drops code on complex files, confirmed: lost 320 lines in a SuggestCommand split). SCOPED 2026-08-13 BY OWNER DIRECTIVE so this stops contradicting on-load step 18: the never-Haiku caution covers SPLITS and broad multi-file restructuring, where nothing in the deliverable reveals a silent drop. It does NOT cover ordinary coding. ALL OTHER CODING GOES TO HAIKU -- a guard edit, a registry row, a seam, a one-line disable -- under the proto-to-live-wiring three-artifact contract, module proto plus WIRED proto that is a byte copy of canonical carrying only the seam plus a self-test. THE CONTRACT IS WHAT MAKES THE DIFFERENCE SAFE: a byte diff of the wired proto against canonical surfaces exactly the loss that went unnoticed in the split incident, so the failure mode that justified the caution is the failure mode the wiring discipline detects. Before this scoping the two skills pointed opposite ways and the owner had to break the tie out loud every session. It does NOT cover ordinary coding. THE CONTRACT IS WHAT MAKES THE DIFFERENCE SAFE: a byte diff of the wired proto against canonical surfaces exactly the loss that went unnoticed in the split incident, so the failure mode that justified the caution is the failure mode the wiring discipline detects. Before this scoping the two skills pointed opposite ways and the owner had to break the tie out loud every session. Default work -> Sonnet inline (no agent needed). Slightly difficult (uncertain, complex, more than 3 tool calls) -> Opus Agent tool. Hard/ambiguous/needs planning -> Triad first, then dispatch the plan to cheap agents.

DISPATCH MECHANICS: fire independent parallel tasks in one message with multiple Agent tool calls. BEFORE BLAMING A TIER, CHECK THE LAUNCHER ITSELF: on 2026-08-13 every delegation in every family failed because WKAppBot/bin/Agent.cmd had acquired a UTF-8 BOM on its first line, so cmd.exe read the opening token as BOM+call and the launcher died before Agent.ps1 ran. The failure looks like a model or routing problem and is neither. It is also TOTAL rather than local, because busy-fleet requires a recent delegation before ROOT may edit protected source, and the only way to satisfy it is this launcher -- so the BOM blocks delegation, which blocks ROOT editing, which blocks fixing the launcher. Recognise it by a stray glyph glued to the first word of the echoed command, confirm with od -c looking for 357 273 277, and clear it with wk-bomfix, which is wk-prefixed and therefore pace and busy-fleet exempt. A SECOND LAUNCHER-LAYER FAILURE, MEASURED 2026-09-04, AND THIS ONE BREAKS A TOOL RATHER THAN A DISPATCH: the agent-brief-guard fires on a TOOL'S OWN INTERNAL DELEGATION, not only on a session's. Running wkhippo recent printed, in the middle of its normal output, Brief needs 3 skill refs; found 0 of 3, followed by Agent.ps1 blocked by harness rc equals 2 -- because that tool calls Agent.cmd internally to translate a search term, and an internal call has no brief and can never have one. The guard exists to stop a session dispatching a context-free agent, which is right; applied to a program's own subprocess it silently removes a feature from a tool nobody was delegating with. THE TELL: a brief-guard refusal appearing in output you did not dispatch. WHEN you see one, do not fix your brief -- find which tool made the call, because the fault is that the guard cannot distinguish a session dispatch from a tool's internal one. AND THE SAME ROUND EXPOSED A COST NOBODY PRICES: a STUDY-LOCK NAMING THE CATALOG'S LARGEST SKILLS MAKES A FILE UNDELEGATABLE. Six consecutive rounds on one source file were killed mid-work while every round on its sibling completed, and the difference was the lock: that file's lock names two of the largest skills in the tree, so a cheap tier spends its whole context paying the toll and dies before the edit. The same lock cost ROOT the two largest reads of its session. THE REMEDY IS IN THE BRIEF, not in the lock: tell the delegate to pay the lock with wkappbot skill read <id> --keep '<phrase>', which satisfies the gate at a fraction of the size. THE GENERAL RULE: before dispatching to a locked path, read the lock and count what it names -- a lock that is affordable for you may be fatal for the tier you are dispatching to, and the failure presents as a mysterious kill rather than as a refusal. AND THE FINISH LINE, owner directive 2026-09-04, given because senior sessions keep forgetting it and given while watching one forget it twice in a single session: DISPATCHING IS NOT COMPLETING, AND COMMITTING IS NOT LANDING. A unit of delegated work is finished only when THREE things have happened, and each has been skipped in this tree within living memory. FIRST, THE SECTORS WENT OUT IN PARALLEL, in one message, rather than one after another -- serial dispatch is not compliance with the delegate rule, it is the shape of a session that will run out of time before its list does, and the descent order names it as the first non-negotiable step. SECOND, THE WIRING WAS CHECKED: the promoted module has a real caller in a production host, and that was proven by LOADING the host in a fresh process and asking whether the function is now defined, never by a parse check -- a parse cannot resolve a dot-source, and this repo has taken its own live harness down for two tool calls by trusting the first for the second. THIRD, IT WAS PUSHED, scoped to the intended paths, because work that never left the machine is work the successor cannot inherit and the defect it fixes stays live. THE REASON THIS BELONGS IN A ROUTING SKILL rather than in a checklist: each of the three is invisible from where the mistake is made. Serial dispatch looks like diligence, a green self-test looks like a working system, and a local commit looks identical to a landed one in every command a session normally runs. So the check is not remembering harder -- it is asking, at the moment you would call something done, which of the three you can PROVE with a command you have already run. Prevent conflicts by giving each agent disjoint FILES -- never isolation worktree and never a branch (owner 2026-09-15). Pass run_in_background true when you do not need the result immediately.

ECONOMICS + MANDATORY DELEGATION: Haiku is roughly 1/25x Opus cost -- route read-only surveys to Haiku, reserve Codex for multi-file edits/splits. Decision shortcut: ask could I delegate this? If yes, MUST delegate; when in doubt, MUST delegate (mandatory, not advisory). A delegated coder is ALWAYS a fresh session loading only the skills its task needs, which is what makes it fast -- dispatching N of them in parallel shortens a bug's total lifespan by roughly Nx, and the conductor's own expensive session must never absorb coding/exploration context it could have sent to one of them instead. CONFIRMED 2026-09-09 in WkAutoQuant: Sonnet is write-frozen on canonical source by the harness itself (emergency-write-freeze fired on a direct Edit to a locked live-trading file, verdict: canonical SOURCE is off-limits to non-pro claude-sonnet) -- so even a small, fully-verified final wiring diff must go through a pro-tier promotion or a dispatched sector, never a direct Sonnet Edit/Write to canonical.

WILLKIM STANDING ORDERS: the conductor (Sonnet or Opus) does not grind mechanical execution directly when a cheaper tier can do it -- Codex types, Haiku reads, Opus reviews/synthesizes; the conductor specs, delegates, and verifies. Always run a parallel fleet when there is backlog: 1 urgent, 1 important, 1 neglected task, fired simultaneously -- idle fleet is wasted capacity.

SAME-TIER BLOCK (live harness guard): X->X (Opus->Opus / Sonnet->Sonnet / Haiku->Haiku) is pure overhead and is BLOCKED. Always CHANGE tier: Opus delegates DOWN (Haiku/Codex/triad); cheap escalates UP (Opus). Stall guards: Opus 7min / Sonnet 6 / Haiku 3, reset on any successful delegation.

ROOT-ELIGIBILITY = CONFABULATION-FLOOR threshold: a tier can serve as a repo ROOT/conductor only if it can honestly self-assess (catch its own errors without supervision). Sonnet is above the floor (self-reflects) so it is root-eligible: conducts its own repo, self-corrects, delegates down. Haiku is below the floor (confabulates without noticing) so it cannot be a root. A Sonnet root still escalates the hardest synthesis/harness/commit decisions up to Opus.

DELEGATION BOUNDARY: skill knowledge-ification and knowledge-tree cross-linking require high judgment and shape what every future intelligence stands on -- prefer doing this work directly (Opus, or a demonstrably-capable Sonnet-front) rather than delegating authorship to cheap models. Cheap tiers CAN do read-only inventory/survey/audit, planning as a partner, guard-message string edits, verification, and mechanical residue -- just not authoring or cross-linking the tree itself.

SONNET-FRONT REGIME + LIGHTWEIGHT OPUS-ESCALATION: Sonnet is the interactive ROOT/front (root-eligible, self-reflects); Opus is an ON-CALL APEX (escalation-only) for architecture/synthesis/irreversible decisions, not the default front. Sonnet->Opus escalation is lightweight: Opus is a one-shot fresh-context consultant, not a blank agent needing the full brief-guard ceremony -- Sonnet hands it the context plus a sharp question, gets the verdict, and the Opus session terminates. Escalation trigger = Sonnet's own uncertainty: the moment Sonnet is unsure, it calls the one-shot Opus immediately.

HARNESS NORTH-STAR -- HAIKU-RELIABILITY FLYWHEEL: the SUCCESS of the Knowledge-Intelligence Harness = orchestrating Haiku (the cheapest capable model) to succeed at ALL AI work at maximum token cost-efficiency. Gates make Haiku work safely; verify-don-t-trust catches Haiku confabs; per-model reflection recurrence-prevention makes Haiku compound-improve -- each clear failure is recorded once and never repeated. DESIGN TEST for any new harness feature: does it make Haiku more reliable, or let more work move safely to the cheapest tier?

See also: agent-dispatch-preflight-pre-research (when a cheap-tier delegation needs cross-file dependency discovery, ROOT pre-traces the exact file:line locations and hands them in the brief -- narrows Haiku's job to assemble-plus-run, matching its actual strength).

MANDATORY POST-FAILURE DUTY (user directive 2026-07-05, prominent placement since this skill is read before every dispatch): when a delegated subagent CLEARLY fails its mission (could not complete, gave up, blocked by a guard, or -- the subtler case -- claims done but skips the mandatory prove-the-artifact/verify step and hands it back to ROOT), ROOT MUST record the failure + recurrence-prevention lesson into THAT model's own reflection skill (haiku-reflection / sonnet-reflection / gpt-reflection / etc) BEFORE the next dispatch of that model, tagged per agent-failure-reflection-gate step 5 (BUG/TODO/IMPROVEMENT/untagged). This is enforced by the harness (agent-failure-reflection-gate blocks the next Agent dispatch on an undetected-clear failure) but ROOT should do it PROACTIVELY even for failure modes the gate's keyword-detection does not catch (e.g. a deferred-verification near-miss is not always a literal 'could not complete' string). See agent-failure-reflection-gate for the full gate mechanics.

BLAST-GATED MERGE AUTHORITY (user 2026-07-10): who does the LIVE connection (merge to canonical) is decided by BLAST RADIUS, not by model. The trap to avoid: 'the pro model (Opus) merges everything' just sanctions the cheap model punting everything = the defer-instead-of-land abdication (and it negates the cheap model's own antidote that wkedit IS its landing tool and it CAN connect canonical). RULE: the executing model LANDS low-blast merges ITSELF via wkedit -- a message-only change, a .md edit, an isolated fail-open helper, an additive log line -- landing is its job; do NOT reflexively defer. Escalate to a pro model for the live connection ONLY on HIGH-blast: a blocking gate, cross-file coordination, a security guard, anything FALSE-BLOCK-capable or that freezes/corrupts broadly if wrong. SELF-TEST before deferring: if this merge is WRONG, does it freeze/corrupt BROADLY, or fail safe + local? broad -> escalate; safe/local -> land it yourself. Punting a safe merge upward is abdication; shipping a catastrophic one unreviewed is a false-completion. Be neither. Pairs with the delegate-expectable handoff criterion (can a fresh autonomous agent be EXPECTED to return this correct from the brief alone?) and the proto-then-review split: build-legwork items -> Sonnet protos+verifies then Opus reviews+merges; diagnosis/design items -> escalate EARLY before the proto, since a proto of a confabulated root-cause is negative value.

POLICY 2026-07-13 (user directive): Opus dispatches for live-file guard/hook changes should be scoped to PROTO-ONLY (build + verify a proto copy, zero canonical edits, zero commits to the live file) -- the actual WIRING into canonical should be done by ROOT directly afterward (fast, using the established wkappbot file edit --old-file/--new-file pattern), or delegated as its OWN separate, narrowly-scoped wiring-only task. REASON: a long-running Opus session (this session saw 5-8 minute dispatches, one burning 605k tokens) that holds BOTH design AND live-wiring responsibility keeps canonical files in a transitional state for a long window, and the agent itself can get gated/blocked mid-task by unrelated harness state changes (live-caught: agent-failure-reflection-gate deadlocked 3 consecutive Opus dispatch attempts mid-session on an unrelated stale-failure record, wasting the whole retry cycle). The pattern that worked smoothly all session: cheap agent (Haiku/Codex) or Opus builds+verifies a PROTO, ROOT does the final live wiring itself in a short, fast, bounded action. Reserve a single long Opus session doing both design AND wiring for cases where the wiring itself genuinely requires ongoing judgment mid-wire (rare) -- default to the split.

CALIBRATION 2026-07-13 (user pushback, valid): ROOT over-reserved Opus for a PROTO-ONLY task on wkharness.ps1 (the single most sensitive live file) purely because of the file's blast radius if the eventual WIRING goes wrong -- but the proto-building step itself touches ZERO live files (only creates new proto/scratch files), so it carries NO live risk regardless of which model builds it. The file's sensitivity is a reason for care during the WIRING step (already policy: ROOT does that personally, see step 14), not a reason to escalate the PROTO-BUILDING step to Opus. Haiku already proved capable of equivalent proto-only extraction work today (gemini/agy family-logic extraction) on other guard files. CORRECTED RULE: model tier for a PROTO-ONLY task should be chosen by task MECHANICAL complexity (checkpoint insertion, straightforward extraction = Haiku-appropriate) regardless of which canonical file the proto targets, since the proto itself never touches canonical -- reserve Opus specifically for the WIRING step when the target file's blast radius genuinely warrants it, or for proto tasks requiring real design judgment (e.g. the CLI-integration Bash-delegation-failure design task, which needed genuine judgment about false-positive risk, not just mechanical extraction).

DECISION: count the GATE COST on both sides before delegating, and TEST the gate rather than inferring it. WHEN: the work itself is tiny (a one-line edit, a two-character change) but the target file looks heavily gated. HOW: attempt the edit yourself FIRST -- one call tells you whether it is actually blocked; only delegate if it really blocks. When you do delegate a gated file, remember the agent must pay that file's study-lock in ITS context, which is the whole point, but it must also be BRIEFED, must re-derive your context, and may misread the spec -- so delegation only wins when the lock cost exceeds the brief cost. WHY: because the delegate-by-default reflex inverts on small gated edits and ROOT got this exactly backwards on 2026-07-15: changing ONE value from 100 to 44 in wkharness-post.ps1 was dispatched to a full agent purely because a DIFFERENT file -- SCOPE LIMIT, added 2026-09-15 after this step misled a session into hand-typing a REORDERING fix (real design judgment, not a value swap) directly into a canonical file's sandbox probe: this step covers ONLY a literal value/typo/constant change with zero design judgment -- if the fix requires deciding new logic, a new regex, a new branch or a changed sequence, that is proto-to-live-wiring step 2's territory (ROOT writes the code INTO A BRIEF, a sector types it), never this step's, regardless of how small the resulting diff looks (wkharness.ps1) had hard-blocked on an eleven-skill study-lock minutes earlier. ROOT never tried the edit -- it INFERRED the block from a sibling file's behaviour. When ROOT finally ran it by hand the edit sailed straight through: wkharness-post.ps1's fourteen-skill list was a PostToolUse keep-fresh NUDGE, not a PreToolUse block, and the two files' gates were never the same gate. Cost of the wrong call: one agent, one brief, one abort message, versus one Edit call. RULE OF THUMB: delegation overhead is roughly a brief plus an agent context plus a verification pass, so anything cheaper than that -- and any edit whose block you have not actually OBSERVED -- is ROOT's own hands. Cross: sonnet-reflection (verify an agent's claim / live-fire is the only proof -- the same do-not-infer-what-you-can-measure discipline, applied to gates instead of guards).

DECISION: DELEGATE THE MEASUREMENT, KEEP THE INFERENCE (2026-07-15, evidence-backed). This is the missing ACTIONABLE COUNTERMEASURE for the confabulation-floor problem this skill already names in its ROOT-ELIGIBILITY step. REFLEX -- TRIGGER: you are about to write a brief containing 'diagnose', 'find the root cause', 'figure out why X fails'. STOP: that brief SHAPE reliably produces a confident WRONG answer from a below-floor tier. DO INSTEAD: convert it to 'run exactly this, paste the complete output verbatim', add an explicit exit contract ('verbatim stdout and nothing else -- no table, no verdict, no root-cause'), and do the inference yourself at ROOT. EVIDENCE (scope it honestly -- this is measured on Haiku, NOT yet on sonnet/codex/gpt): four consecutive Haiku dispatches on one workstream, each given a DIAGNOSE-shaped brief, all four substituted code-reading for execution and returned confident wrong causes -- one claimed 'confidence HIGH' on code it never ran; one said 'only the thresholds need calibration' (ROOT lowered the threshold; it still failed, refuting it); one did 'careful static code analysis', printed zero values and ENDED BY ASKING THE QUESTION IT WAS SENT TO ANSWER; one produced an OK/BROKEN table whose ticks were INFERENCES dressed as measurements, its single falsifiable cell ('would return Block=true') being the exact opposite of ROOT's measured value. The 5th dispatch, same subject matter but re-scoped to measurement-only, came back flawless and settled the question in one shot. THE POINT: the fix was the BRIEF SHAPE, not the model -- the identical model produced perfect data once inference was made impossible rather than merely discouraged. A tell to grep for in any agent report: the word 'would'. Cross: haiku-reflection steps 24-25 (the four incidents + the validated countermeasure), verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static (parse-clean and a green self-test are not proof), agent-cmd (brief construction).

DECISION: NEVER gate DELEGATION on a file-hygiene score -- the only agent who can fix the block is the one the block forbids. WHEN: a guard refuses an Agent dispatch because CLAUDE.md, a skill, or any maintained artifact scores below a cleanliness threshold. HOW: run wkappbot skill read harness-diet-score-guard for the measured stall this produces and wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto before trusting any score you did not print yourself, then move the enforcement to the STOP hook where the debt is genuinely due and leave dispatch as WARN-ONLY -- harness-diet-score-guard step 12 already specifies exactly that split, and the live code hard-blocks at dispatch instead. WHY: measured 2026-07-30, the diet gate refused every delegation at 53, and four rounds of real compression moved it 53-55-58-59 and then STALLED at 59 across a further substantial cut -- reproducing step 7's record of a prior session burning eight turns and five commits on the identical curve. The remedy the block message itself prints is Agent.cmd, which the same block forbids, and its documented escape wkcodex.sh was measured silently no-oping the same day, so the gate is a closed loop: recording a finding grows the file, which blocks the tool needed to act on the finding. A hygiene score is a real signal and belongs at session end; at dispatch it only converts a housekeeping debt into a work stoppage.

TODO: audit every live defence that constrains DELEGATION and report which tiers are actually gated, because the owner's finding on 2026-08-01 is that blocking one tier just moves the behaviour down one step -- opus was blocked and the traffic went to sonnet within the hour, and sonnet gets used whenever the owner is not watching. WHEN: deciding whether the delegation economics are actually enforced, or before adding yet another per-model ban. HOW: run wkappbot skill read claude-code-agent-tier-routing then inventory the guards by NAME, FILE:LINE, TRIGGER-TOOL and the verbatim first sentence of each block message, reading the trigger from the code condition rather than inferring it, and in the same pass list which NON-CLAUDE families (gemini, agy, codex, the ask-triad web tier) are reachable as targets today -- the cheapest real answer to an over-priced Claude tier is usually another family, not a cheaper Claude. WHAT WOULD PROVE IT: a synthetic payload per tier fired at the live hook showing which decision each one gets, since a guard that reads strict in source and never fires is the exact failure this repo has paid for repeatedly. CONTRACT for the fix that follows: gate on the PROPERTY (reaching past the cheapest capable tier without a reason) rather than on a model NAME, and make the escape a CLOSED LIST of tokens rather than free text, because a free-text justification is satisfied by inventing a plausible sentence. Landed so far: E10 blocks opus as a delegation target and E11 requires WHY-NOT-HAIKU with one of four tokens, both in tools/wkharness-guards-emergency9.ps1, self-test 123/123 and live 9/9. PARTIAL AUDIT 2026-08-25 (Sonnet, real grep-based inventory, not guessed): tools/wkharness-guards-agent.ps1 alone carries 9 distinct guard classes across 16 Block() call sites gating every Agent dispatch -- agent-leak-guard (L75), agent-skill-update-guard (L148), agent-debrief-gate (L174/176/187/327, 4 sites), spec-todo (L214), agent-brief (L225/232/236/243/246, 5 sites), reflex-pulse-gate (L265), opus-budget (L278), opus-pace-emergency (L305), clean-baseline (L385). This is ONE file of several in the Agent-dispatch chain -- CORRECTED same session after checking: wkharness-guards-agent-debrief.ps1 (913 lines) and wkharness-guards-busyfleet.ps1 (190 lines) carry NO Block() calls of their own, they are pure decision-logic modules consumed BY wkharness-guards-agent.ps1's Block() sites already inventoried above. The REAL second busy-fleet enforcement site is wkharness-guards-infra.ps1:396-406 (consumes Test-WkBusyFleetNarrowedWhitelist, gates arbitrary Bash/PowerShell/shell_command execution) -- DISTINCT from a THIRD site, wkharness-common-tier.ps1:237 (tag [busy-fleet], gates direct Edit/Write to a study-lock-registered SOURCE FILE, separate code path, separate message). IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE for the 2026-08-25 harness:safe feature (commit a1b88f99f): it only affects site 2 (Bash/PowerShell commands) -- a harness:safe-declared tool does NOT exempt a direct source-file Edit/Write from site 3's busy-fleet gate. Full cross-file inventory still incomplete but growing: wkharness-guards-infra.ps1 alone adds 6 more distinct guard classes across 9 more sites (watchdog L103, pending-protect L116, stall-guard L248/252, bg-task L304/305, busy-fleet-guard L463/483/485 -- note this tag differs from the [busy-fleet] tag in wkharness-common-tier.ps1:237, likely the SAME logical gate's actual message-emission site, unconfirmed), and wkharness-common-tier.ps1 adds study-lock-v2 (L260) beside its own busy-fleet site. Running total across 3 files: 17+ distinct guard classes, 27+ Block() sites. This audit is genuinely large -- a successor continuing it should grep 'Block "\[' across the remaining tools/wkharness-guards-*.ps1 files not yet touched (wkharness-guards-write.ps1, wkharness-guards-git*.ps1, wkharness-guards-shell*.ps1, wkharness-guards-security.ps1, wkharness-guards-stop*.ps1) for the same file:line:tag inventory, rather than re-deriving what is already cited here.

DECISION (owner directive 2026-08-01, BINDING -- the delegation-side twin of the separation rule): when the work touches a FAT source carrying MANY study-lock skills, ROOT does not edit it and does not read its way in. ROOT delegates the SEPARATION. WHEN: the target file is over the line cap, or its study-lock answers with four or more distinct file-specific skills, or you catch yourself about to read a long lock list just to change a few lines. HOW: brief a cheap tier, haiku by default, for exactly THREE deliverables and nothing else -- (1) the one function or logic block lifted VERBATIM into its own new source module with no behaviour change, (2) a WIRING PROTO that is a byte-copy of canonical carrying only the seam, so the seam is diffable before it lives anywhere, (3) a runnable SELF-TEST asserting BOTH directions, the case that must fire and the case that must not. Where the file only needs cutting, the zero-token deterministic splitter replaces any hand-split. ROOT reviews the diff for additions-only, re-runs the self-test from its OWN seat, and performs the merge -- the canonical merge stays ROOT's charge. THE TRAINING LOOP: a wrong or incomplete return is NOT a reason to take over. Diagnose why YOUR brief failed, correct it, re-dispatch, and repeat until the agent returns it right -- that loop trains the agent AND trains ROOT's briefing, and the arithmetic favours it heavily since one expensive tool-call is worth roughly twenty cheap ones. WHY: the owner gave this after watching a session try to hand-edit an eleven-lock guard file and get study-locked out of a two-line repair. Taking over would have burned the expensive seat on mechanical work AND skipped the training round that makes the next dispatch land first time. Cross: harness-source-edit-requires-skill-lock (the separation-side twin, where the lock-count trigger is defined).

HALF YOUR DELEGATES RETURNING EMPTY IS NOT A REASON TO STOP DELEGATING, and the owner had to catch me twice on 2026-08-14 before I counted. WHAT I TOLD MYSELF: dispatches kept returning a zero-byte file at exit zero, so I called delegation unreliable HERE and started hand-editing, turn after turn, tunnelling one file serially. THE ACTUAL TALLY, run only when challenged: twenty-two dispatches, eleven empty, eight with real usable output. Fifty percent is not zero -- and the half that worked was the most valuable work of the session. TWO OF THOSE EIGHT CORRECTED ME on findings I had already published: one located the real block log after I sampled the wrong file and told the owner blocks were never recorded, and one read sixteen modules to quantify a drift as twenty-one of twenty-seven where I had estimated and understated it. Neither was reachable by hand in reasonable time, and both changed conclusions I was about to build on. THE ASYMMETRY IS THE ARGUMENT: an empty return costs one dispatch and nothing else -- no context, no wrong direction, no bad artifact. A delegate that DOES return supplies breadth and INDEPENDENCE I structurally cannot produce alone, because I check my own work with my own assumptions. Expected value stays strongly positive at a fifty percent hit rate, so the correct response to empties is MORE parallel dispatches, never fewer. THE TELL TO WATCH FOR IN YOURSELF: the moment you justify hand-work with an ADJECTIVE like unreliable rather than a NUMBER, stop and count. I was wrong by a factor one command would have shown. AND THE OWNER'S PROPOSED REMEDY, which I agree with and record here as a design: BAN EDITING OUTRIGHT DURING THE DESCENT. His words were that Opus cannot fix this habit, and he is right that two verbal corrections did not fix it. This fleet has only ever cured a repeating class by REMOVING THE OPTION, never by advice -- the four environment-variable backdoors ended by deletion, not by persuasion. A descent-scoped edit ban removes the judgement call I keep getting wrong, which is whether to delegate or to type. THREE CARVE-OUTS ARE REQUIRED or the descent becomes impossible: the handoff letter, which IS the deliverable, the rules file's pending list, and commit plus push. Everything else routes to a sector. His words were that Opus cannot fix this habit, and he is right that two verbal corrections did not fix it. This fleet has only ever cured a repeating class by REMOVING THE OPTION, never by advice -- the four environment-variable backdoors ended by deletion, not by persuasion. A descent-scoped edit ban removes the judgement call I keep getting wrong, which is whether to delegate or to type. THREE CARVE-OUTS ARE REQUIRED or the descent becomes impossible: the handoff letter, which IS the deliverable, the rules file's pending list, and commit plus push. Everything else routes to a sector. TWO RECORDS DISAGREE AND I WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS BEFORE FINDING THE SECOND -- read this whole entry before acting on any part of it. FIRST I proposed restoring the wkharness_INTERNAL_SPAWN environment marker as a fix. THEN I found the removal commit and retracted hard, calling it a deliberate backdoor removal. THEN I read wkharness-guards-write.ps1 around line 201 and the picture changed again. That comment says the flag was adopted to REPLACE an expensive ancestor-walk costing 400 to 800ms per Edit, and that it was chosen SPECIFICALLY BECAUSE it is not the model-identity env backdoor which gpt-reflection forbids -- so in that file it was reasoned about as the SAFE option, not the dangerous one. A further note dated 2026-08-02 in the same block gives the decisive fact: the variable is NEVER SET ANYWHERE, because the native Agent tool's subagent is spawned by the Claude Code SDK, outside this repository, so no script here can put an environment variable on that process. THAT ALSO KILLS MY WRITER-HALF PLAN: Agent.ps1 does not spawn the native subagent, so a line added beside it could never reach one. THE HONEST STATE IS A CONFLICT, and recording it beats resolving it by preference: proto-cleanup-discipline calls this variable a backdoor that a commit gate was hiding, while wkharness-guards-write.ps1 calls it the deliberately-non-backdoor choice. Both are in the knowledge base, both are dated, and I do not know which reading the removal commit acted on. WHAT I ACTUALLY LEARNED, and it is the transferable part: my conclusion reversed twice in one hour on one subject, and NEITHER reversal came from reading more code. Each came from finding ONE MORE RECORD -- a commit message, then a comment block in a fourth file. When a mechanism looks broken, the missing information is usually not in the implementation; it is in whatever someone wrote down when they changed it, and those writings can contradict each other. Do not act until you have found at least two and reconciled them. DO NOT ACT ON THE REPORT BELOW. I proposed restoring an environment marker named wkharness_INTERNAL_SPAWN so delegates would stop being classified as ROOT. Then I ran git log with the -S flag on the constant and found commit e319b075a, chore(harness): replace remaining WKHARNESS_INTERNAL_SPAWN environment references with constant 0, authored by an Opus session. The constant is not a regression, an oversight, or an unfinished feature. IT IS A DELIBERATE BACKDOOR REMOVAL. Confirmation was already in a skill I had READ THE SAME SESSION: proto-cleanup-discipline records that the cheap-source-guard commit gate HID a WKHARNESS_INTERNAL_SPAWN env backdoor. That variable belongs to the same family this repo has torn out three times -- the model-stamp spoof, the busy-fleet kill switch, the diet override -- where any process that can set an environment variable can declare itself exempt from the guards. MY FIX WOULD HAVE REINSTATED IT, and I had written it up as a careful cross-repo report with file, line and evidence, which is exactly how a bad change acquires credibility. WHAT I GOT WRONG METHODOLOGICALLY, stated so it transfers: I treated three source COMMENTS pointing at an env check as documentation of intent, when they were documentation of a PAST implementation nobody updated when it was deliberately removed. Stale comments made a security decision look like a bug. THE CHECK THAT CAUGHT IT COSTS ONE COMMAND -- before restoring anything that looks accidentally disabled, run git log with -S on the disabling text and read the commit MESSAGE. A chore-labelled commit is still a decision. THE ACCURATE FRAMING, after reading the commit itself: git show on e319b075a dates it 2026-06-28, by Opus, touching four files, and its title says REMAINING references -- the tail of a larger removal. So the identity detector returning a constant is a six-week-old deliberate security decision, and delegates being classified as ROOT is its ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE, not a defect anyone introduced by accident. THAT DISTINCTION CHANGES WHAT TO DO. A defect gets repaired. An accepted consequence with an unpaid cost gets a DESIGN decision: either the cost is worth bearing and the guards that fire wrongly on children should be scoped so they cannot, or a forge-proof identity source replaces what was removed. Both are real options and neither is a bug fix. WHAT NOBODY DID, and this is the actual gap: the removal took away the signal and left every ROOT-only guard consulting a function that now always says ROOT. The security half was completed and the usability half was never started. A removal that is correct can still be unfinished. So the identity detector returning a constant is a six-week-old deliberate security decision, and delegates being classified as ROOT is its ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE, not a defect anyone introduced by accident. Both are real options and neither is a bug fix. The security half was completed and the usability half was never started. A removal that is correct can still be unfinished. THE REAL PROBLEM SURVIVES AND NEEDS A DIFFERENT ANSWER: delegates genuinely are misclassified as ROOT, confirmed twice live through root-post-delegation-mtime firing on a haiku child. The fix must derive child identity from something a process CANNOT set about itself -- process lineage, the payload the harness itself writes, an agent id issued by the spawner -- never from an environment variable the child could forge. CROSS-REPO REPORT, superseded, kept only as the record of what I nearly did: the subagent identity marker is missing and it costs every delegation in this repo. CONFIRMED TWICE LIVE 2026-08-14, through two different gates and two different briefs: a haiku child was refused by root-post-delegation-mtime, a guard that exists to tell ROOT to consume its delegate's output. A child cannot be ROOT, so its firing on a child proves the child was classified as the parent. THE READER HALF, in THIS repo and already proven: wkharness-common-classify.ps1 defines Test-WkInternalSpawn as a hardcoded constant false -- literally a comparison of two different literals -- so it can never return true, and five live guards consult it. A corrected version comparing the process environment entry wkharness_INTERNAL_SPAWN against the digit one has been built and exercised in both states. THE WRITER HALF LIVES IN ANOTHER REPOSITORY, personal-docs, beside Agent.ps1 line 150 where the parent already sets wkharness_AGENT_MODEL for its child -- a channel PROVEN to work, since three post hooks read that variable successfully. One line setting the marker beside it completes the pair. THIS IS A REPORT BECAUSE THE FILE IS NOT MINE. Per the scope rule, a defect found across a repository boundary is handed to that repo's owner with file, line and evidence -- never edited from here, because a commit lands in a tree whose in-flight state you cannot see. LAND BOTH HALVES IN ONE CHANGE OR NEITHER: the reader alone yields a function reading a variable nobody sets, which is the same permanent false it replaces, and the writer alone sets a variable nobody reads. ALSO FIX THE COMMENTS IN THE SAME CHANGE -- three of them in wkharness-guards-infra.ps1 describe this mechanism as live, which is why it took a full session to find something that was never working.

DECISION: A DELEGATE WITH BAD POSTURE IS DISCARDED, NOT COACHED -- kill that session and re-dispatch a FRESH one with a sharper brief. Owner ruling 2026-08-25. THE TEST IS TWO QUESTIONS AND THE SECOND ONE IS ARITHMETIC, clarified by the owner the same day after a session over-applied this rule within minutes of learning it. DISCARD when (1) the agent is being STUBBORN -- it substituted its own judgement for an explicit instruction and would do so again -- or (2) REPAIRING IT COSTS MORE TOKENS THAN STARTING OVER, which is the whole of the criterion and not a feeling: weigh the cost of sending the correction against the cost of a fresh session re-reading its skills and re-staging its files. If continuing is cheaper, CONTINUE. THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE, measured 2026-08-25: a brief was truncated in delivery and the agent reported the exact cut point and asked for the missing EDIT blocks. That is neither stubbornness nor expensive repair -- it is the CHEAPEST possible case, since only the missing fragment had to be sent, and the agent had already paid for its four mandatory skill reads. ROOT discarded it anyway, throwing away that context and paying for a whole new session to redo work that was already done. An agent that asks a precise question about a defect in ROOT's OWN input is not misbehaving; it is reporting a ROOT-side fault, and the fix is to answer it, not to replace the asker. WHEN: the returned work shows the agent substituted its own judgement for an explicit instruction -- it was told to reuse a named module and wrote its own arithmetic instead, it was told never to call get_token and called it, it was told to copy a file and hand-wrote a shorter one, or it reported a check it never ran. HOW: do NOT SendMessage a correction into that session; dispatch a NEW agent whose brief opens by naming the previous failure and the measurement that exposed it, and read wkappbot skill read proto-to-live-wiring-howto step 1 for the rule that the FIRST instruction of any brief is the extraction proto. Reserve SendMessage for a genuine SPEC CHANGE, where ROOT learned something new and the agent's posture was never the problem. WHY: posture is a property of that session's whole transcript, so a correction lands in a context that has already normalised the shortcut, and the same substitution reappears one layer down. Measured 2026-08-25, four times in one session: a 978-line file returned as a 241-line hand-written fragment reported 4/4 PASS; a self-test that re-implemented the seam it was meant to bind to; a required hide-the-dependency run omitted from the report entirely; and a price module that emitted 13,832.5 on a five-won tick grid while passing 8/8, its own report stating it had skipped the wk_price import it was told to reuse. Every one was caught by ROOT running one command against the artefact, and every one was cheaper to re-dispatch than to repair in place.

DECISION: discard a coder session and dispatch FRESH whenever re-instructing it would cost more tokens than a new brief, or whenever the coder has turned stubborn -- owner ruling 2026-08-27, given in two parts, first that if the tokens to work from a NEW instruction are fewer than the tokens to correct the coder by re-instruction then throw that coder session away and delegate again with a fresh mind, and second that a stubborn coder does get drawn now and then. WHEN: a delegate returns something wrong and you are about to type a correction into the same session. HOW: price the two paths before replying -- run wkappbot skill read proto-to-live-wiring-howto for the brief template, and ask whether the defect is a TYPO in the work or a DESIGN the brief failed to specify; a typo is worth one correction, a wrong design means the whole brief must be rewritten anyway, so the resume buys nothing and carries the old wrong model as dead weight. Kill it and dispatch a brief that names the missing spelling, marked THIS IS A FRESH ROUND so the new coder does not go hunting for the discarded work. WHY: measured the same day. A seam came back reading a resting order's PRESENCE as a fill with a hardcoded 1, where the owner's own specification calls for the TRACKED ORDER'S QUANTITY -- a design gap my own brief created by never naming the source, so correcting it in place would have meant retyping the whole specification into a session that already held a wrong model of the task. THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is why this is arithmetic rather than a licence to churn: opus-self-reflection step 1 records discarding a coder that had honestly reported a truncated brief and asked for the missing fragment, which is the CHEAPEST possible resume and exactly the case to keep. Honest confusion is cheap to fix; a wrong design and genuine stubbornness are not. MECHANISM LIMIT measured the same day, and it collapses the arithmetic to one branch on this dispatcher: an Agent.cmd dispatch CANNOT BE RESUMED. A coder correctly reported that FILE 1 of its brief was cut off mid-docstring and asked for the fragment rather than inventing one -- exactly the keep case -- and SendMessage to its task id returned no agent named that is reachable, because Agent.cmd spawns a shell process that has already exited by the time the completion notification arrives; only in-process Agent-tool subagents are addressable. So for Agent.cmd the cheap path is not a resume but a CORRECTED BRIEF FILE plus re-dispatch, whose marginal cost is one edit rather than a rewritten specification. THE TRUNCATION CAUSE WAS THE BRIEF'S OWN: it contained a triple-quoted Python docstring, and the triple quote is what cut the read -- write a plain hash comment in any brief that shows Python, and believe a delegate that quotes the exact cut-off point.

THE REASON IS ARITHMETIC AND THE OWNER GAVE IT PLAINLY ON 2026-09-10: IF ROOT WRITES THE CODE, THE REVIEWER COUNT DROPS TO ONE. His words were that when you do the work there is only one inspector left, so will it turn out right. A delegate plus ROOT is TWO independent readings of the same contract; ROOT alone is one reading twice, and a misreading in the head that wrote the code is invisible to the eyes that then review it. So the rule is not merely about cost -- delegating the WRITING is what BUYS the review, and doing it yourself spends the reviewer to save the typist. MEASURED THE SAME DAY, both directions in one hour. THE MODEL WORKING: a sector was handed a stale wiring proto, read a brief phrase as an instruction to replace a line rather than add beside it, and moved to overwrite a LIVE rate limiter -- ROOT caught it by reading the running transcript, killed the sector, and the host measured clean afterwards. THE MODEL BROKEN: ROOT then wrote that seam BY HAND instead of re-dispatching with a sharper brief, and no second reader existed for it. THE SAME HOUR PROVED THE REVIEW IS WORTH REAL MONEY: a delegate returned a 43-case suite at exit 0 that ROOT accepted only after RUNNING it, and the run exposed a hardcoded absolute path inserted at sys.path position zero -- which breaks on every fresh clone AND makes the null-action control structurally impossible, so the suite could never be made to fail and was therefore not evidence. Neither defect is visible in a passing tally; both are visible in ten seconds to a second reader. THE OPERATING SHAPE: delegate the writing, run the artifact yourself, and when it is wrong REDISPATCH with the exact correction named rather than fixing it in your own seat. THE ORIGINAL RULE FOLLOWS. DECISION: CODING GOES DOWN, WIRING AND VERIFICATION STAY AT ROOT, and getting that backwards is a real failure rather than a style choice. Measured 2026-08-31 in wkappbot-kih, owner said it twice: I hand-wrote a guard module -- five KB of PowerShell, on the expensive seat, slowly -- and then wrote a brief handing the SEAM to a haiku. That is the inversion exactly. The module is mechanical work with a stated contract, which a cheap tier returns as two protos plus a suite for a fraction of the tokens; the seam DECIDES WHAT EVERY OTHER INTELLIGENCE THEN RUNS and is the one thing a cheap tier must never touch. THE TELL IS THE COST SHAPE: if you are typing implementation while a delegate waits for instructions, you have swapped the halves. And delegating the module also buys two independent verifiers and a confidence figure, which doing it yourself buys neither. ORIGINAL STEP FOLLOWS. DECISION: do it yourself when YOUR cost is lower than the junior's TOTAL cost, and the junior's cost is not just their tokens -- it is LEARNING TOKENS DIVIDED BY (LEARNING PROBABILITY times SELECTION PROBABILITY) -- the tokens they burn coming up to speed, divided by the chance they actually understand the task once briefed and the chance the deciding skill is even selected into their context. DIVISION, NOT MULTIPLICATION, and the owner had to correct me on exactly this: a probability is always below 1, so MULTIPLYING makes the junior look CHEAPER the less likely they are to succeed, which is the opposite of the truth. Dividing is also the principled form -- at success probability p the expected number of attempts is 1 over p, so the expected cost is tokens over p. AND THE NUMBER IS NOT A PRICE TAG, IT IS A LEARNING BURDEN -- owner's own framing, and it changes what the formula is for. The quotient is how much the junior must ACTUALLY absorb to succeed at this specific item, not an abstract cost, so the question it puts to ROOT is not which is cheaper but WHETHER THAT LEARNING IS POSSIBLE AT ALL. Ask it in that order: compute the burden, then ask if it fits -- inside the junior's context window, inside their tier's capability, inside a brief you could realistically write. When the burden exceeds what they can hold, the verdict is not expensive, it is IMPOSSIBLE, and ROOT does it with no further deliberation. Only when the learning genuinely fits do you go on to compare it against your own cost, then act without pausing to ask. WHEN: every time you are about to write a brief, before the first line of it. HOW: run wkappbot skill read claude-code-agent-tier-routing-howto for the briefing recipes, then ask the three questions in order -- how many tool calls is this really, would a junior plausibly get it RIGHT, and does the deciding knowledge reliably reach them; if the second or third is shaky the delegation is a lottery ticket and doing it yourself is the cheap move. WHY, and the owner has now said it twice because he is tired of repeating it: a fifty-line brief was written to delegate a three-command timing measurement and the brief alone cost more than the work. THE CASE THAT SHOWS THE OTHER TWO TERMS, measured 2026-08-29: three unbounded transcript reads had to be classified as safe-to-bound or not, and getting one wrong meant a guard that runs FASTER AND BLIND -- Get-WkEvidencePriorRefCount counts across the WHOLE session with no time window, so a tail silently erases an early read, while its two neighbours are genuinely boundable. A junior briefed to apply a fixed tail to all three would have shipped that, because the brief itself would have carried the wrong instruction. Low learning probability on a semantics judgement is exactly when the multiplication says do it yourself. NOT A LICENCE TO HOARD: bulk reads, surveys, multi-file refactors and long mechanical work still go out, because there all three of the junior's terms are high and yours is the one that is bad.

RESULT: the learning burden does not have to be estimated -- the harness ALREADY BILLS IT, and the study-lock is the invoice. To edit a locked source file anyone, senior or junior, must first read that file's locked skills, so the SUM OF THOSE SKILLS' SIZES is the measured learning burden for touching that one spot, and a junior pays exactly the same toll. WHEN: sizing any delegate-or-do-it call on locked source, which in this repo is nearly all of it. HOW: run wkappbot skill read claude-md-harness-rules for how a study-lock is declared, then read the lock block for the target file and add up what it names -- that sum is the numerator, before any probability divides it. WHY: measured on this session 2026-08-29, twenty-five oversize knowledge outputs alone persisted to 1620 KB, roughly 415k tokens, and that EXCLUDES every skill read that landed inline. Applying the owner's own observation that both probability terms sit under one half in almost every real situation, the divisor falls under 0.25 and the burden clears 1.6M tokens, past any junior's context window by an order of magnitude -- so the verdict is IMPOSSIBLE by arithmetic rather than by taste. THE SHARPER FORM OF THE SAME TEST: if writing the brief means doing the thinking, there is nothing left to delegate; that is what an IMPOSSIBLE looks like from the inside, and it is why three guard defects found this day had to be fixed by ROOT rather than dispatched.

DECISION: the senior side of this comparison is NOT a constant, it is CUMULATIVE, and leaving it out inverts the answer late in a session. Every tool call re-sends the whole transcript, so senior cost is TRANSCRIPT SIZE times NUMBER OF CALLS while the junior pays their learning burden ONCE in a fresh context. The crossover is therefore a moving line, not a property of the task. WHEN: any delegate-or-do-it call, and especially when you catch yourself reusing a judgement you made earlier in the same session. HOW: run wkappbot skill read claude-session-handoff for why a session hands off at all, then compute both sides with the CURRENT transcript size rather than the one you started with -- delegate when transcript times expected calls exceeds the junior's burden. WHY: measured on this session 2026-08-29 by the owner's correction. At 5.1 MB the transcript is about 1.34M tokens RE-SENT PER CALL, while the junior burden for the same work measured about 1.6M once. So two calls already cost 2.68M and the crossover had ALREADY PASSED -- the identical task that was correctly mine at session start belonged to a junior by the end, same judgement, same files, different clock. THE CONSEQUENCE WORTH CARRYING: a senior session gets monotonically worse at doing things itself, which is exactly why the descent ritual exists and why a session past the size line should be handing knowledge over rather than grinding. Do not read an early-session do-it-yourself verdict as still valid later; recompute it.

DECISION: the handoff letter is not documentation, it is the LEVER ON THE DENOMINATOR -- and this closes the whole formula. Learning probability sits UNDER the division bar, so every point the letter raises it DIVIDES the successor's burden and moves the crossover, making work delegable that was IMPOSSIBLE before. The skill tree, the anchors and the study-locks do the same job for selection probability. That is what this harness IS: a machine for raising the two terms in that denominator. WHEN: writing a handoff letter, or wondering whether a paragraph in one earns its space. HOW: run wkappbot skill read claude-session-handoff for the letter's own contract, then judge each passage by one question -- does this raise the chance a fresh reader UNDERSTANDS AND ACTS, or is it merely true. A passage that is true and inert is a passage that lowers nothing. WHY: measured 2026-08-29, and the measuring instrument already exists. wkareyouready --Start hands the letter to four fresh intelligences and asks what they DO, which makes it a live probe of learning probability. That run: four of four read well, ONE of four verified anything, and ZERO acted -- so p-learn for reaching ACTION was about zero, and the predecessor's brand-new AND THEN ACT section had failed to move it on a single reader. A letter that produces understanding without action has not raised the term that matters. THE COROLLARY FOR THE SENIOR SIDE: since senior cost only grows and junior burden only shrinks as the letter improves, time spent making the letter teachable is the single highest-leverage act available late in a session.

DECISION: the session's choice set for delegation is EXACTLY ONE model, the youngest; escalation is the SYSTEM's decision under its own internal rules, never a session judgement. WHEN: choosing which tier to dispatch to. HOW: wkappbot skill read claude-code-agent-tier-routing-ref for historical context and samjil-prevention lessons, then verify the SYSTEM decided tier escalation (never the session), then verify in this repo's CLAUDE.md section THE INTELLIGENCE MAY DELEGATE TO THE YOUNGEST ONLY that the pattern rule is narrower than its scope statement. WHY: E11 demanded a closed-list token to escalate past haiku, but the model choosing the token is already the model that decided, inverting the constraint; when the youngest cannot do work, the fault is IN THE BRIEF -- convert diagnose-shaped briefs to run-exactly-this-and-paste-output, name the ONE directory it may write, and re-dispatch, or hand to another FAMILY's youngest.

DECISION: before delegating N units of work, ask whether N is the ANSWER or whether one boundary question collapses it -- the delegate instinct fires on VOLUME, and volume is exactly what a badly framed question produces, so a large fan-out is evidence to examine rather than a routing signal to obey. WHEN: a task presents as many similar units (classify 44 files, audit 30 rows, check every entry) and the obvious move is a fan-out or a single agent looping. HOW: run wkappbot skill read foundation-is-roots-charge-not-a-chore for the sibling rule that persistent balance between options means the SHAPE is wrong, then spend one cheap command asking what the units have in common before you brief anyone -- ls the set and ls the place their answers would live, and see whether the population partitions. Delegate only what survives the partition. WHY: measured 2026-08-31 in personal-docs. I burned TWO delegations on classifying 44 leftover protos; the first returned 39 of 41 marked ORPHAN with an evidence cell left as a literal ellipsis, the second punted by spawning a sub-agent against an explicit brief constraint and sat waiting for it. Then two ls calls -- one over the proto names, one over the other repo's tools folder -- showed that roughly two thirds are named after wkappbot-kih tools, so their canonicals live in a repo this session may not edit and NONE of them was ever a blocked promotion here, while the rest are one-off portal scripts with no canonical at all. The real deliverable was one sentence about a boundary, and no amount of correct per-file diffing would have produced it, because every row would have been individually right and collectively beside the point. THE TELL I MISSED TWICE: I was briefing a method (how to diff) when I had never checked the population (what these files ARE). A delegate given a good method on a mis-framed set returns a well-executed wrong answer, which is more expensive than a refusal because it looks finished.

DECISION: the Haiku-versus-Codex line is not about SIZE, it is about whether the edit is ARGUMENT VALIDATION IN EXISTING CODE -- that is source work however few lines it costs, so route it to Codex on the FIRST dispatch. WHEN: a delegate has returned rc=0 twice on the same explicit defect list and the defects still standing are all phrased as ABSENCES -- a missing guard, an unvalidated argument, a type never rejected -- while the one it keeps re-solving is the one it already understood; also whenever your brief asks a cheap tier to HARDEN an existing function rather than to add a new one. HOW: stop re-briefing and escalate -- run wkappbot skill read agent-cmd for the dispatcher form, then re-send the IDENTICAL brief with --model codex, and afterwards run wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto and probe the artifact OUTSIDE its own suite before believing any tally. WHY: measured 2026-09-03 in WkAutoQuant. A ten-line numeric validator inside ONE function -- reject bool by type, reject NaN and infinity with math.isnan and math.isinf, reject a non-positive cap -- went to Haiku twice with a numbered defect list, each defect carrying the exact failing call and the exact required output dict. Round one fixed one defect of four; round two fixed the same one again and left the other three, exiting rc=0 both times. The identical brief handed to Codex fixed all four in one round and the nine-line hostile-input probe then matched byte for byte. Adding a branch to code that already exists reads to a cheap tier as a smaller task than it is. ONE CODEX BEHAVIOUR TO EXPECT SO IT DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A LOSS: it TRUNCATES the target file to zero bytes before rewriting, so a poll inside that window shows an empty file -- this one went 11812 bytes to 0 to 7356 within a minute and the final content was correct, so wait for the completion notification before concluding the work was destroyed.

requirements.expect: the separation-side twin, where the lock-count trigger is defined: four or more distinct file-specific study-lock skills means separate the logic into its own module rather than editing the fat source in place

the final-artifact acceptance pattern a returned delegation is judged against: git-mv promotable whole file, diff showing only the intended change, no BOM or line-ending drift, parse-clean, and a self-test that asserts the block MESSAGE text and would FAIL if the proto were reverted
the four terms in one place, so a router does not have to reassemble them from steps 24-28
the ten-part brief shape, plus the walls-with-commands rule and the brief-is-the-log rule that a dispatch needs when the CLI has no resume path
